title: Sanada Yukimura Never Signed "Yukimura"? 4 Letters｜Curio Archive
description:
Sanada Yukimura of games and taiga dramas: did he ever call himself "Yukimura"?
For anyone who loves Sengoku history, has played Sengoku games, or wonders where historical names come from.

In 1917 (Taisho 6), Tokyo Imperial University's Dai Nihon Shiryo printed one of his letters as a plate titled "Letter of Sanada Yukimura", yet the letter is signed "Sanada Saemon-no-suke Nobushige".

His letters from inside Osaka Castle are signed Nobushige or with his title, Saemon-no-suke; a letter from Kudoyama asking someone for shochu is signed "Kohaku Nobushige". He died in battle at Osaka on the 7th day of the 5th month of Keicho 20 (June 3, 1615). A letter by Hosokawa Tadaoki, on the enemy side, calls him "Sanada Saemon-no-suke"; a postwar report kept by the Shimazu family passes on the line "Sanada, the finest warrior in Japan", but the text itself says only "Sanada Saemon" and "Sanada", and the small "Yukimura" beside it was added later. The first work to write "Yukimura" is generally thought to be the Naniwa Senki (preface dated 1672); in the Togen Iji, compiled after Tokugawa Mitsukuni's death, the editor wrote in a small note that calling him Yukimura is wrong. In 1809 the Sanada family drafted an answer saying it was the name he used after entering Osaka, while admitting no book recorded the change. In 1911 (Meiji 44) Tatsukawa Bunko published "Chibo Sanada Yukimura", priced at 25 sen.

No document from his own time found so far says "Yukimura"; who first gave him the name, and why, is still unknown. The letters follow the Dai Nihon Shiryo transcriptions; the Naniwa Senki we read is a later expanded and reprinted edition, so whether the original had "Yukimura" cannot be confirmed. Dates in the narration follow the old lunar calendar; "I think" and "we think" are this channel's views. Sources are listed below.

Data as of 2026-10-20

sv103.text: But surprise: of the letters in his own hand we've found, none is signed "Yukimura."

sv104.text: In 1917, a Tokyo Imperial University source book printed one of his letters as a plate.

sv106.text: But at the end of the letter, he signs: Nobushige. Title and signature differ by a whole name.

sv109.text: When the shogunate asked in 1809, the Sanada family drafted an answer first.

sv212.text: "Kōhaku"? Where's that name from? Keep it in mind.

sv213.text: Later, he left Kudoyama, entered Osaka Castle, and stood against the Tokugawa.

sv302.text: It opens: someone's passing, so a note.

sv303.text: Was Muramatsu his older sister? That's the usual view, but even Edo-era genealogies disagree.

sv306.text: Heavier still: on the 10th of month two, set to hold the castle, he wrote Ishiai Jūzō:

sv307.text: we're holding the castle, so I've resolved to die;

sv316.text: Then his monogram, a signature drawn as a design.

sv318.text: Under two months after that letter, on the 7th of month five, he died at Osaka.

sv319.text: Researchers say his commendations to six men, the day before he died,

sv320.text: were on small wooden pieces like shogi tiles, still signed Nobushige.

sv401.text: One of them was in the enemy camp: the daimyo Hosokawa Tadaoki,

sv402.text: who wrote home on the 15th, calling him "Sanada Saemon-no-suke,"

sv403.text: and said his feat was unmatched in all history.

sv404.text: But the most famous line isn't in Hosokawa's letter.

sv405.text: A post-battle report kept by the Shimazu names him too;

sv406.text: dated the 11th of month six, just over a month after his death.

sv407.text: The fighting had just ended, news was still on the road; was it reliable?

sv408.text: The print we read lacks its opening and has no signature.

sv409.text: Who wrote it? It's filed among the family records of the lord Shimazu Iehisa;

sv410.text: but filed there doesn't mean Iehisa wrote it; the writer left no name.

sv411.text: Remember "Japan's finest warrior"? It's in this report:

sv412.text: Sanada, Japan's finest warrior, unmatched in any tale of old.

sv413.text: The sentence ends with "yoshi," meaning: it is said.

sv414.text: It adds this was all anyone talked about.

sv415.text: So was this verdict the writer's own opinion?

sv416.text: No; the report ends by saying it records rumors from the men below.

sv417.text: It even hedges: if anything differs, a correction will follow.

sv418.text: Seeing "I heard" in a group chat, you'd doubt it a bit, right?

sv419.text: And what does the report call him? Also by title: "Sanada Saemon," or simply "Sanada."

sv420.text: But in the print, by "Sanada Saemon," stand two small characters:

sv421.text: Yukimura: the later addition I mentioned at the start.

sv422.text: Who added them is unclear; likely they date from when it was copied.

sv423.text: That's strange: the writer never wrote this name, yet someone added it beside his.

sv424.text: So which book first put the name "Yukimura" in writing?

sv501.text: The earliest is thought to be a chronicle of the Osaka war: the Naniwa Senki.

sv502.text: Its preface was written in 1672, fifty-seven years after the Osaka war.

sv503.text: Fifty-seven years: your grandpa's birth to your youth, right?

sv504.text: It says: Masayuki of Ueda Castle's second son, Saemon-no-suke Yukimura.

sv505.text: But why he's called Yukimura, the book never says.

sv506.text: You might think: so "the year it started" is the preface's year?

sv507.text: I thought so at first. But we can't say it yet.

sv508.text: That preface was for the two original authors.

sv509.text: What we read is a copy someone later expanded; the person who did it left no year.

sv510.text: It was reprinted in 1928, and the notes say inverted phrases were rewritten in kana and wording revised.

sv511.text: We can't tell if the original had "Yukimura."

sv513.text: Yes. Tokugawa Mitsukuni of Mito died in month 12 of Genroku 13: early 1701.

sv514.text: After he died, Mito retainers compiled his words and deeds as the Tōgen Iji,

sv515.text: drawn from his personal doctor's notes.

sv516.text: It quotes Mitsukuni calling Sanada "Nobu" with another second character.

sv517.text: Here's the catch: right under that name, the editors added a note in small characters:

sv518.text: calling him Yukimura is a mistake. That's the editors talking, not Mitsukuni.

sv519.text: Clearly, by then "Yukimura" had spread so far that someone had to correct it.

sv520.text: Notice? Even "calling him Yukimura is a mistake" is written small, to the side.

sv521.text: But does the name they gave match his letters?

sv522.text: It doesn't; that name appears nowhere in his letters.

sv523.text: Later, the essay Okinagusa wrote that Mitsukuni himself looked into it and said Yukimura was wrong.

sv524.text: We think even "who said Yukimura was wrong" was later rewritten once.

sv525.text: Outsiders said Yukimura was wrong; how did the Sanadas record him?

sv601.text: Remember the Sanada family's later draft genealogy?

sv602.text: The entry it gives him is filed under "Yukimura."

sv603.text: Beneath it, it says: first called Nobushige; on Mount Kōya, he went by Kōhaku.

sv604.text: The "Kōhaku" on the shōchū letter was his mountain name.

sv606.text: a shogunate inspector asked about Sanada genealogy.

sv607.text: One question was: was Nobushige his original name?

sv608.text: As a Sanada retainer, asked about an ancestor from nearly 200 years ago, what would you say?

sv609.text: The Sanadas first drafted a memo on how to answer: yes, Nobushige was his original name.

sv610.text: And if they then asked about "Yukimura"?

sv611.text: The drafted answer: he used that name only after leaving the family to join Osaka;

sv612.text: at home he was always called Nobushige. But does that answer hold up?

sv613.text: Those 1615 Osaka letters? It came after joining,

sv614.text: yet they're signed Nobushige, or Saemon-no-suke.

sv615.text: Not one says Yukimura. Honestly, that's strange.

sv616.text: The same memo honestly admits one thing:

sv617.text: his change of name to Yukimura can't be found in any book.

sv618.text: These are just memos; what was sent, we haven't seen.

sv619.text: So is there a letter he signed "Yukimura" himself?

sv620.text: Two copies have come down, with no originals; researchers judge both to be forgeries.

sv621.text: Per the editors' note, the official Kansei Chōshū Shokafu also has "Yukimura, first named Nobushige."

sv622.text: How did a name even his family couldn't source become nationwide?

sv702.text: Tatsukawa Bunko published volume five: Chibō Sanada Yukimura.

sv703.text: Priced at 25 sen; in the same ad, volume one was Ikkyū Zenji.

sv704.text: I think picking him in a game and Meiji readers paying 25 sen for him are the same thing:

sv705.text: so the first name we all meet is "Yukimura."

sv706.text: And so, "Sanada Yukimura" became a name known across Japan.

sv707.text: Its origin still unexplained, the name had run on ahead.

sv708.text: Not over yet. Remember the 1917 sourcebook we began with?

sv710.text: even the shōchū letter has a margin note: Yukimura asks for shōchū.

sv711.text: The Shimazu report got his death date off by a day; editors fixed it;

sv712.text: guess what the note calls him? Yukimura, again.

sv713.text: Back then, scholars called him Yukimura.

sv714.text: We think that plate's title records exactly what that era called him.

sv801.text: Today, researchers combing reliable sources from his life

sv802.text: also say: not one of them uses "Yukimura."

sv803.text: So, back to the opening question: did he ever call himself "Yukimura"?

sv804.text: Who first used it, and why, we still don't know after all these records;

sv805.text: but whether he used it, the records can answer.

sv806.text: To Muramatsu, Ishiai, and his brother-in-law: Nobushige or Saemon-no-suke.

sv807.text: I think others can write a name again and again; but what he signed himself was never that name.

sv808.text: Of the documents from his time found so far, none says "Yukimura"; this file: archived.

sv809.text: Well, that's today's story. Where did you first hear "Sanada Yukimura": a game, a TV drama, or a book?

sv810.text: Tell me in the comments. We stick to the records; subscribe to open files with us.
